label: Pesher Nahum (Commentary on Nahum) — Complete
summary_plain: Pesher Nahum is a commentary on the prophetic book of Nahum, applying its words to events in the community’s recent history. The commentary identifies the ‘lion’ as a historical ruler who invited foreign armies into the land. It speaks of the ‘seekers of smooth things’ who led the people astray in Yerushalayim. The Kittim are the foreign power from the west. The pesher interprets the fall of Nineveh as a prophecy of the fall of the corrupt Jerusalem establishment. YHWH’s judgment against Nineveh is YHWH’s judgment against every institution that oppresses his covenant people.
summary_scholarly: 4QpNah (4Q169 — Pesher Nahum) is a continuous commentary (pesher) on Nahum 1-3, found in Qumran Cave 4. The text is historically significant because it contains some of the most explicit historical references in the Dead Sea Scrolls, mentioning identifiable figures and events. The ‘seekers of smooth things’ (dorshei hakhalaqot) are likely the Pharisaic movement. The ‘lion of wrath’ who ‘hangs men alive’ is generally identified with Alexander Jannaeus (103-76 BCE), who crucified 800 Pharisees. The Kittim are the Romans. The pesher method reads the prophetic text as a cipher for contemporary events — every verse of Nahum has a current referent. This hermeneutical approach is unique to Qumran and differs from both later rabbinic midrash and Christian typology.

key_terms.definition: Commentary on Nahum — 4QpNah, a continuous pesher applying the book of Nahum's oracles against Nineveh to the Qumran community's own time. Remarkable for being the only DSS pesher to name actual historical figures rather than code-names.

Demetrius III Eucaerus — the Seleucid king named in Pesher Nahum, who invaded Yehudah around 88 BCE at the invitation of internal enemies. This is one of only two or three places in the DSS where a historical figure is named by their actual name.

Code name in Pesher Nahum for a Hasmonean ruler — almost certainly Alexander Jannaeus (103-76 BCE), who crucified 800 Pharisees. The 'lion' who 'hangs men alive' — the crucifixion reference is explicit in the text.

In Pesher Nahum, Kittim refers to Rome — an identification confirmed by the text's historical context. The term originally meant Macedonians/Greeks but shifts in the DSS to refer to Rome as the dominant foreign power.

Code name in Pesher Nahum for a group the community opposed — widely identified as the Pharisees, based on the pun: 'smooth things' (halaqot) sounds like 'laws' (halakhot) with the consonants rearranged, implying the Pharisees substituted smooth/easy rulings for the Torah's demands.

Pesher Nahum col.1:7-8 contains the DSS's most explicit reference to crucifixion — 'hanging men alive' — applied to the Lion of Wrath (Jannaeus). This is the earliest known non-Roman text that describes crucifixion as a political execution method in Yehudah.

The Cave 4 designation for Pesher Nahum — 4Q169. The 'p' prefix stands for 'pesher' (commentary). Found among the Cave 4 pesharim alongside commentaries on Yesha'yahu, Habakkuk, Psalms, and other texts.
Another title in Pesher Nahum — may refer to a successor or alternate epithet for the same Lion of Wrath figure, or possibly to a different Hasmonean ruler in the same period.

Code names in Pesher Nahum for two opposing groups within the community's social landscape — sometimes identified as Pharisees (Ephraim) and Sadducees (Menasheh). These tribal names function as identity labels in the pesher's reading of Nahum.

Pesher Nahum reads Nahum's oracles against Nineveh as prophecies about the community's contemporary enemies. Nineveh becomes a type for all imperial/corrupt power — the pesher method maps ancient oracle onto present reality.

faq.question: What is Pesher Nahum?
faq.answer: Pesher Nahum (4QpNah, 4Q169) is a continuous commentary on the book of Nahum from Cave 4. It applies Nahum's ancient oracles against Nineveh to the Qumran community's contemporary situation — the Hasmonean period and early Roman involvement in Yehudah. It is remarkable for being the only DSS pesher to name actual historical figures (Demetrius III, the Lion of Wrath understood as Alexander Jannaeus) rather than relying entirely on code names.

faq.question: Why is the crucifixion reference in Pesher Nahum significant?
faq.answer: 4QpNah col.1:7-8 describes the Lion of Wrath 'hanging men alive' — a clear reference to crucifixion. This is the earliest known non-Roman literary reference to crucifixion as a political execution method in Yehudah, predating Roman direct rule. The reference is applied to Alexander Jannaeus's mass crucifixion of 800 Pharisees around 88 BCE. The DSS document this event in a way that no other surviving ancient text does in the same detail.

faq.question: Who are the Seekers of Smooth Things?
faq.answer: The Seekers of Smooth Things (dorshei halaqot) is a code name that plays on the Hebrew words for 'smooth things' (halaqot) and 'laws' (halakhot). The community accused this group of substituting smooth, easy legal rulings for the Torah's demands. They are almost universally identified by scholars as the Pharisees, based on the pun and the historical context of the rivalry between the Pharisees and the community that produced the DSS.

faq.question: What does Kittim mean in Pesher Nahum?
faq.answer: In the earliest DSS texts, Kittim referred to Macedonians/Greeks (the Seleucids). By the time of Pesher Nahum and the War Scroll's later layers, Kittim refers to Rome. The term migrated as the dominant foreign power changed. This shift helps scholars date the composition of different DSS texts — if Kittim = Greeks, the text is earlier; if Kittim = Romans, the text is later.

faq.question: How does the pesher method work in Pesher Nahum?
faq.answer: The pesher method takes an ancient prophetic text (Nahum's oracles against Nineveh) and reads it as a coded prophecy about the community's own time. Nahum never mentioned Demetrius or the Pharisees — but the pesher interpreter sees through the ancient oracle's surface meaning to its 'true' referent in contemporary events. The method assumes that all ancient prophecy was encrypted foreknowledge of the community's situation.

faq.question: What historical period does Pesher Nahum reflect?
faq.answer: The late Hasmonean period — primarily the reign of Alexander Jannaeus (103-76 BCE) and the events surrounding his rule, including the Pharisee-Sadducee civil conflict, the invitation of Demetrius III, and the mass crucifixion of Pharisees. The text may also reflect the beginning of Roman involvement under Pompeius (63 BCE). It is a document produced from within a turbulent political moment, reading that moment through Nahum's ancient lens.

faq.question: Who is Demetrius in Pesher Nahum?
faq.answer: Demetrius III Eucaerus, the Seleucid king who invaded Yehudah around 88 BCE. He was invited by internal opponents of Alexander Jannaeus (Pharisees according to Josephus). After defeating Jannaeus in battle, Demetrius withdrew, and Jannaeus then crucified 800 of the Pharisees who had supported the invasion. Pesher Nahum reflects on this sequence of events, reading them through Nahum's oracle.

faq.question: What are Ephraim and Menasheh as code names in Pesher Nahum?
faq.answer: Ephraim and Menasheh are the two tribes of Yosef's sons — here used as code names for two groups the community viewed as rivals or enemies. Scholars most commonly identify Ephraim as the Pharisees and Menasheh as the Sadducees, though the identifications are debated. The use of tribal names as code names is consistent with the DSS's practice of encoding contemporary identities in biblical typology.

faq.question: How does Pesher Nahum help date other DSS texts?
faq.answer: Because Pesher Nahum names Demetrius (around 88 BCE) and refers to the Lion of Wrath's crucifixion (Jannaeus, around 88 BCE), it anchors the community's historical context in the late Hasmonean period. This date range — late 2nd to early 1st century BCE — becomes a reference point for dating other texts that share the same code names and historical anxieties. It also confirms that the community was active observers of Hasmonean politics.

faq.question: Why is Pesher Nahum important for understanding the NT period?
faq.answer: The crucifixion reference in Pesher Nahum shows that crucifixion was a known and dreaded form of execution in Yehudah before the Roman period — it was used by the Hasmonean rulers themselves. The DSS community's horror at the Lion of Wrath's crucifixions documents a cultural memory that shapes the entire period. Additionally, the Pharisees who appear as the 'Seekers of Smooth Things' in this text are the same group whose legal tradition eventually became Rabbinic Judaism — Pesher Nahum documents the community's sharp opposition to that lineage.
